weaknesses: Practical content of the 'explicit', 'calibrated', 'operational' claims (abstract; introduction paragraph 4; Discussion paragraph 5). The lower and upper multipliers are astronomically far apart: k_v = 2^{-17}(2*2^{40})^{-S} against C^att_v >= 16*1024*sqrt(A_*). Size 0.0075 comes from Chebyshev bounds with a 2^{16} cutoff factor, the test is identically zero at n = 2, 3, and N^att_v = ceil((2C^att_v/d_0)^{1/E}) is far beyond any data set. The sentence that the thresholds 'give the rate statements an operational interpretation' therefore oversells. Fix: describe the test as a rate-attaining construction with conservative explicit constants, report the magnitude of C_v/c_v and N_v at one or two representative tuples, and move the practical-constant gap into the Limitations subsection.

Assumption discussion is formulaic and omits the restrictions that drive the results (Section 3.2). Each assumption is followed by a sentence saying it is 'a fixed-envelope version' of a condition in Kennedy et al. Nothing explains (i) why gamma >= 1/4 is imposed and what fails below it; (ii) why all smoothness exponents are capped at 1, which excludes the higher-order regime where histogram projection is suboptimal; (iii) whether the numerical envelopes 20, 10, 1/2, [1/4, 3/4] are normalizations or matter; (iv) why a raw rather than centered conditional moment is bounded; (v) how the known uniform design is used: the ordered-pair correction needs no density or Gram-matrix estimation, so E_4 may not survive an unknown design. Fix: add a paragraph per item, and say in the introduction that the rough-confounding exponent is derived for a known design.

Positioning omits the closest technical antecedents (Sections 1-2). The ordered-pair projection correction is a second-order U-statistic of higher-order-influence-function type, and the copula-frame lower bound, with coupled propensity and outcome perturbations whose product carries the signal, mirrors the Robins-Li-Tchetgen Tchetgen-van der Vaart construction for semiparametric minimax rates. Neither is cited; only Kennedy et al. (2024) is. Also uncited: heavy-tailed minimax mean estimation and truncation (Catoni; Bubeck-Cesa-Bianchi-Lugosi; Devroye-Lerasle-Lugosi-Oliveira), which is where the q = (p-1)/p exponent comes from, and the econometric heterogeneity-testing literature (Chernozhukov-Demirer-Duflo-Fernandez-Val; Ding-Feller-Miratrix; Levy et al. on the variance of the CATE). The link between E_0(2) = 2*gamma/(4*gamma+1) and the classical Ingster rate appears only in an appendix. Fix: add these comparisons to Section 2, state which rate components are new (the p < 2 interaction and the alpha/beta asymmetry in E_4), and move the Ingster comparison into the introduction.

The two rate exponents are stated but never explained (Section 1 and the prose after the main theorem). The reader is told that E_4 'incorporates the interaction of propensity and baseline regularity', but not why alpha enters as 2*alpha while beta enters as beta/q, nor why F(p) has 2*alpha/(p-1). The asymmetry comes from clipping the outcome but not the treatment indicator. Fix: add a short heuristic derivation in Section 4 balancing bias K^{-S}, clipping bias T^{1-p}, variance T^{2-p}*sqrt(M)/n and the second-order variance term. Also rename E_0 and E_4, whose indices suggest missing E_1 to E_3.

The main theorem is a seven-bullet omnibus that restates the notation, mixes headline results (matched radii, tail region) with bookkeeping (positivity of constants, existence of an open set U, compact uniformity), and has upper constants defined only through an appendix theorem. The broader-class and original-class supplied-propensity theorems are near-verbatim duplicates, with near-verbatim duplicate proofs, although the text itself notes the second follows from the first by class inclusion plus the common witnesses. Fix: state one short rate theorem (two-sided radius bound plus the phase rule), one corollary for the cost of tails, one for the preservation boundary; put tail-essentiality in its own theorem; derive the original-class supplied-propensity result as a corollary of the broader-class one.

The cost-of-tails framing should concede what the benchmark comparison does and does not isolate (Sections 4 and 7). The 'bounded benchmark' is |Y| <= 1, compared with a raw p-th moment bound of 10. At p = 2 the finite-variance class already has the bounded rate, so the penalty is specifically for moments strictly between 1 and 2, not for unbounded outcomes. Applied outcomes such as earnings or expenditures usually have finite variance. Fix: say this in the abstract and introduction ('finite variance suffices for the bounded-outcome rate; each moment order below two costs a polynomial factor') and discuss which applications have p < 2.
